White-Label Web Development: Manage Change Requests Without Losing the Brief

Help agency reviewers separate corrections, defects and new scope while keeping website changes traceable and ready for client approval.

By SiteSutra · 28 October 2026

← All articlesYour next step ↓

A white-label website project can slow down when every comment becomes an urgent instruction. The developer may not know whether a note corrects the approved brief, reports a defect or asks for additional work. The agency may approve a change without seeing its effect on responsive layouts, accessibility, timing or other pages.

A useful change-request process keeps the client relationship with the agency while giving the delivery team one traceable decision path. It does not remove conversation; it records the decision that comes out of it.

Start with an approved delivery baseline

Before implementation begins, record the approved page list, design source, copy version, required states, integrations, reviewer and acceptance checks. This baseline makes later requests easier to classify. Without it, “please fix this” can mean a missed requirement, a preference change or a new feature.

Name the person who consolidates agency feedback. Client comments can remain visible to the agency, but the development queue should receive one approved instruction when comments conflict. Record which person can approve scope, delivery-date or commercial changes.

Classify the request before estimating it

Four starting categories for agency review
CategoryWhat it meansEvidence to check
DefectThe delivered behaviour does not meet the approved brief or acceptance check.Expected result, actual result, page, device and reproducible steps.
Content correctionApproved business information needs an accurate replacement.Verified replacement text or asset and the person who approved it.
ClarificationThe reviewer needs an explanation before deciding whether a change is required.The exact question, affected state and current implementation.
Scope changeThe request adds or changes an agreed page, component, integration or responsibility.Business reason, dependencies, impact and explicit approval.

The category is a starting point, not a way to reject feedback. A small wording request may affect repeated components or metadata. A visual defect may reveal that the approved design did not include a required mobile state. Investigate the affected area before confirming effort or timing.

Write a request the developer can reproduce

  • Location: page URL, section or component.
  • Current result: what the reviewer can see or do now.
  • Expected result: the approved behaviour or requested outcome.
  • Context: device, viewport, browser and relevant account state.
  • Evidence: screenshot, recording or approved content source when useful.
  • Decision owner: the agency reviewer authorised to approve the final instruction.

Keep account credentials, private client messages and customer data out of the request. Use the platform’s access controls when a developer needs authorised access to reproduce an issue.

Hypothetical example: an agency landing-page build

Imagine a fictional design agency supplying an approved desktop and mobile landing page for implementation. This is an original planning example, not a SiteSutra client project or delivery result.

During review, the client asks for a different phone number, reports that the mobile navigation covers the heading and requests a new testimonial carousel. The agency records the phone number as a content correction with an approved source. It records the navigation overlap as a defect with the device width and steps. The carousel becomes a scope change because the approved brief contains a static proof section and no permissioned testimonial set.

The developer corrects the phone link and navigation in the next preview. The agency decides separately whether to quote the carousel after confirming content permissions, controls, responsive behaviour and accessibility requirements. One review round can therefore close two agreed issues without silently expanding the implementation.

Use one review path from preview to acceptance

  1. Log the request and assign its owner.
  2. Confirm the category and reproduce the current result.
  3. Record affected pages, components and dependencies.
  4. Approve any change to scope, timing or commercial terms before implementation.
  5. Provide a reviewable preview and identify the exact change.
  6. Retest the original acceptance check and related states.
  7. Close the request with evidence or return it with a specific reason.

A repository pull request is one possible review surface when the project uses Git. GitHub’s pull-request review guidance supports line comments, suggestions, approvals and requests for changes. The buyer-facing benefit is a visible proposed change before it reaches the production branch. The actual review tool should match the agency’s delivery workflow.

Retest more than the changed pixels

A change to navigation, forms, headings, colour, motion or interactive controls can affect people who use a keyboard, zoom, reduced-motion settings or assistive technology. Add the relevant checks to the request instead of leaving accessibility for the final handover.

W3C recommends evaluating accessibility early and regularly throughout design and development and tracking findings in the normal quality-assurance process. W3C also notes that tools alone cannot determine full accessibility. Record the tests actually performed rather than making a broad claim from one automated result.

Keep revisions and new scope commercially clear

The delivery agreement should explain the included review rounds, what counts as correction or defect work, who can approve additional work and how timing is reassessed. Avoid promising that every request will fit the original milestone before its dependencies are understood.

For a time-sensitive request, record the business deadline and the smallest safe release. A temporary workaround, if agreed, should include an owner and removal date. Urgency does not remove the need to review production risk.

Download the agency change-request register

Download the white-label website change-request register (CSV). It includes clearly labelled hypothetical rows and fields for location, category, expected result, evidence, impact, owner, approval, preview, acceptance check and status.

Replace the examples with verified project information. Keep credentials, customer data and confidential client content in the systems approved for that project.

Agree the change path before the first review

Add the change categories, reviewer, approval authority and acceptance evidence to the agency brief. Then use the same register from the first preview through handover.
